newsitem.title: GERMANY: Feuding public, private banks greet EU resolution.
newsitem.headline: Feuding public, private banks greet EU resolution.

text.p: Germany's public and private banks, disputing whether state money received by public banks broke EU subsidy rules, both claimed victory on Wednesday following a European Union resolution granting a limited special status for public banks.
EU leaders meeting in Amsterdam on Tuesday agreed to a German request to exempt publicly-owned regional banks, or Landesbanken, from EU competition rules.
But the resolution fell short of Bonn's call for a full exemption and applies only to the public tasks carried out by the Landesbanken.
The association representing private banks, the Federal Association of German Banks, said it was satisfied that the Amsterdam summit had not enshrined full state protection for the Landesbanken.

Tuesday's decision paved the way for an EU investigation into billions of marks of public money received by the Landesbanken, the association, which includes banking giants like Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank, said in a statement.
"The public sector can only compensate the Landesbanken and savings banks for those costs that result from their public tasks," it added.
But Germany's DSGV savings bank association issued a statement welcoming the fact that the German government had made the public service function of the public banks clear at the Amsterdam summit.
"The savings bank association sees its position confirmed...that the organisation and activity of the savings banks and Landesbanken are fully in line with European competition rules," the DSGV said.
An EU probe would call into question Germany's giant public sector banking system, which is backed by state gurantees and therefore enjoys top credit ratings.

The increasingly acrimonious dispute dates back to 1994 when the private banks filed a complaint with the Commission saying 11 billion marks of state capital transferred to Landesbanken since 1990 constituted a breach of EU subsidy rules.
The capital transfer resulted from the integration of various state-owned housing development agencies into the Landesbanken.
The private banks see that transfer as distorting competition because it gave regional banks capital at a far lower price than that charged for funds in the private sector.
They were also opposed to the Bonn government's request for a resolution fixing the system of state protection in EU law.
The Landesbanken are owned by their respective federal states and savings bank associations.
They act as clearing institutions to the savings banks and do not offer retail banking services but they do compete with private banks in corporate finance, securities trading and issuing.
